These results demonstrate that dynamic codes outperform standard methods by avoiding highly noisy components, even without physical defects, while preserving logical boundaries. Our findings challenge the conventional dependency on static fault-tolerant architectures by verifying the feasibility and efficacy of the LUCI framework on physical hardware and pave the way for hybrid, hardware-compatible code designs in quantum computing.

papers.title: Macroscopic Quantum Tunneling in Superconducting Junctions: Theoretical Aspects
papers.journal: Journal of Superconductivity and Novel Magnetism

papers.title: Gradiometric, fully tunable C-shunted flux qubits
papers.abstract: Abstract Fully tunable flux qubits offer in-situ and independent controls of their energy potential asymmetry and tunnel barrier, making them versatile tools for quantum computation and the study of decoherence sources. However, only short coherence times have been demonstrated so far with this type of qubit. Here, we present a capacitively shunted flux qubit featuring improved relaxation times up to T 1 = 25 μ s and a 20-GHz wide theoretical frequency tunability range at the flux-insensitive sweet spot, of which a 3-GHz range was shown. As a model application, we demonstrate detection of two-level tunneling defects in a frequency range spanning one octave.

papers.title: Surface code logical operations on a superconducting quantum processor
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires logical operations that manipulate encoded information while preserving quantum error-correction protection. In planar surface-code architectures, code deformation and lattice surgery provide a local, measurement-based route to such operations. Here we experimentally realize key elements of patch-based surface-code logical processing on a 107-qubit superconducting quantum processor. We first implement a reusable primitive layer comprising merge and split, patch expansion and shrinkage, and deformations mediated by domain walls and twist defects. We then compose these primitives to realize logical state routing, the logical controlled-NOT gate, and the single-qubit Hadamard and phase gates, which together form a Clifford-generating set. All operations are implemented on distance-three rotated surface-code patches with multi-round syndrome extraction and neural-network decoding, without post-selection. Our results advance superconducting surface-code experiments from protected logical memory to active, patch-based fault-tolerant logical operations.

papers.title: High-Precision Calibration Workflow Achieves Above $99.9\%$ CZ Gate Fidelity on a Scalable Superconducting Processor
papers.abstract: High-fidelity universal two-qubit gates are critical for building fault-tolerant quantum computers. In scalable superconducting processors, shortened coherence times introduce more incoherent errors in gate operations. With a constrained error budget, there is reduced tolerance for coherent errors stemming from parameter deviations. In this work, we develop a closed-loop workflow to enhance the CZ gate calibration precision. Utilizing the echoed leakage error amplification (ELEA) and the repurposed context-aware fidelity estimation (CAFE) circuits, we suppress the population leakage to non-computational states, and, for the first time, demonstrate a CZ gate fidelity exceeding $99.9\%$ on an 84-qubit processor, with coherent error suppressed to $0.007\%$. Meanwhile, we obtain a median fidelity of $99.25\%$ among 72 CZ gates, demonstrating that the workflow can be generalized to the calibration of parallel CZ gates. Finally, we realize automated calibration and observe enhanced stability of the CZ gate throughout 9-hour comparative monitoring experiments. Our results, realized on a completely domestic platform, establish an efficient and automated route to quantum computation with superconducting quantum systems.

papers.title: Bit flips are erasures in dissipative cat qubits
papers.abstract: Autonomous quantum error correction (QEC) stabilizes a logical manifold through dissipative events that emit into output channels, which are typically accessible to measurement. These signals are often discarded, and whether they contain useful information about logical failures remains generally unclear. Using quantum trajectories, we show that in dissipatively stabilized cat qubits bit flips are not silent logical errors: each flip is accompanied by a strong, time-localized photon burst from the dissipative buffer. Photon counting and homodyne monitoring can therefore herald the loss of logical information without interrupting the autonomous stabilization: bit flips in dissipative cat qubits are erasures. More broadly, our results show that the emitted signals of engineered reservoirs can act as built-in failure monitors for autonomous QEC, turning rare logical faults into erasures available to a decoder and reducing fault-tolerance overhead. To this end, we develop a general framework, based on past quantum states and number-resolved master equations, to quantify the detectability of such logical failures in autonomous QEC from the emitted signal.

papers.title: Symmetry Classification of Non-Reciprocal Responses in Multiterminal Ring Devices
papers.abstract: We present a symmetry-based framework to classify the non-reciprocal responses of multiterminal ring quantum devices. The device is modeled as a ring of $n$ vertices, where a binary variable $e_k\in\{+1,-1\}$ on each bond encodes the preferred direction of signal flow between terminals. Non-reciprocity corresponds to a preferred current configuration on the ring, and the symmetry group of the device partitions all $2^n$ configurations into equivalence classes(orbits) characterized by a topological winding number $W$. Using the minimal non-trivial case $n=3$, we establish two results independent of microscopic details. First, lifting the degeneracy within an orbit generates non-reciprocal responses. For $n=3$ this requires simultaneous breaking of both time-reversal $T$ and spatial inversion $I$. Breaking either alone is insufficient. Second, the residual geometry symmetry after $T$ and $I$ are broken determines which responses are observable. For an isosceles triangular geometry, only two types of response are allowed: uniform circulation (all bonds carrying current in the same direction) and semi-circulation with the reversed bond on the geometrically distinct base. Semi-circulation with the reversed bond on either equal leg is symmetry-forbidden. Both predictions are validated using a minimal toy model of three quantum dots coupled to superconducting baths, which demonstrates a reactive quantum circulator response.

papers.title: Characterization of Hydroxyls in Surface Oxide of Superconducting Tantalum and Their Mitigation in Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Recently, tantalum (Ta) has gained attention in superconducting quantum circuits due to the longer coherence times achieved when replacing niobium (Nb) in capacitor pads. Previous literature shows that surface oxides that form upon ambient exposure on superconducting metals such as Ta, Al, and Nb host two-level system (TLS) defects, which are a leading source of microwave loss and decoherence. While the surface oxides of Nb and Al have been extensively studied, Ta oxides remain less well understood. Using secondary ion mass spectrometry of alpha-Ta films deposited at 300 mm wafer scale, we show for the first time that hydroxyls accumulate in the Ta suboxide region above the underlying Ta. Angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy shows that the surface region is dominated by Ta2O5, with sub-stoichiometric TaOx present in between the Ta2O5 and underlying Ta. The thickness of the tantalum oxide is confirmed by transmission electron microscopy. We demonstrate that [OH] incorporation can be suppressed by replacing the native oxide with an oxide formed during chemical mechanical planarization of alpha-Ta films. Our findings support the hypothesis that TLS defects are non-uniform within the oxide thickness and suggest hydroxyls as a probable molecular origin of these loss channels. Furthermore, we show the feasibility of plasma nitridization as a method to decrease hydroxyl loading on alpha-Ta surfaces. The modulation of hydroxyl content through surface engineering of alpha-Ta can enable the fabrication of more robust, high-coherence superconducting quantum circuits by addressing a potential TLS source.

papers.title: Vanadium superconducting microwave resonators on silicon wafers
papers.abstract: Understanding the correlation between material properties and microwave losses in superconducting films is a crucial subject for developing low-loss materials for quantum circuits. We focus on vanadium (V) as a novel material for superconducting quantum devices and discuss loss in V films in relation to their structural properties. Using a sputtering method, we grow four V-film structures on (001)-oriented Si wafers, employing Nb and Ta as the buffer and capping layer materials, respectively: Nb/V/Ta, Nb/V, V/Ta, and V. X-ray diffraction and atomic force microscopy reveal that the V films grown on the Nb buffer layers have higher uniformity of lattice orientation and smaller grain size than that directly grown on the Si wafer. Coplanar waveguide resonators are fabricated from the four V-film structures, and averaged photon number ($\langle n_{\rm ph} \rangle$) dependences of internal quality factor ($Q_{\rm int}$) are obtained by performing microwave measurements. By analyzing the obtained $Q_{\rm int}$ vs $\langle n_{\rm ph} \rangle$, it is found that loss at the V surface is dominated by $\langle n_{\rm ph} \rangle$-independent non-two-level-system (non-TLS) losses, which can be mitigated by introducing the Ta capping layer. Furthermore, the V films on the Nb buffer layers exhibit lower $Q_{\rm int}$ in the $\langle n_{\rm ph} \rangle$ range from 10$^{0}$ to 10$^{6}$ and higher non-TLS loss than that directly grown on Si wafers, even though the former has higher lattice-orientation uniformity than the latter. Origins of these trends might be relevant to V oxides, of which presence at surfaces and grain boundaries in bulk regions in the V resonators is suggested by energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and/or V hydrides.

papers.title: Bias-Preserving Gates and Quantum Error Correction With Dual-Rail Cat Codes
papers.abstract: Scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation requires quantum error-correcting codes that simultaneously support universal logical operations, suppress hardware-specific noise, and enable efficient handling of photon-loss errors. Bosonic encodings such as the dual-rail and cat codes each offer attractive features but also exhibit important limitations when used in isolation. The dual-rail code enables efficient single-photon-loss detection by converting leakage out of the computational subspace induced by photon-loss errors into an erasure error. In contrast, the cat code provides a resource-efficient, bias-tailored error-correction scheme with bias-preserving logical gate operations. Here, we introduce the dual-rail cat code (DRCC), a concatenated bosonic encoding that combines an inner cat code with an outer dual-rail structure, thereby inheriting and enhancing the advantages of both constituent codes. We analyse the error-correction properties of the DRCC and propose a deterministic single-photon-loss correction protocol by concatenating it with an outer repetition code. Exploiting the code's intrinsic noise bias, we construct a universal set of logical gates using only beam-splitter interactions and demonstrate that all logical operations preserve the erasure-biased noise structure. The DRCC offers several distinctive advantages, including the absence of relative geometric phases during gate operations, deterministic erasure detection and correction, and simultaneous syndrome extraction without interrupting stabilisation. These features make the DRCC a promising bosonic code for hardware-efficient, bias-preserving, and erasure-resilient fault-tolerant quantum computation.

papers.title: Experimental Quantification of Layered Error Suppression in Fiber-Interconnected Quantum Data Centers
papers.abstract: We perform experiments to quantify error suppression in fiber-connected superconducting QPUs using combined error mitigation techniques, demonstrating over 20\% improvement in operational fidelity across interconnected quantum processing units under realistic noise conditions.

papers.title: Leakage Mobility and Passive Leakage Removal in Transmons with Tunable Couplers
papers.abstract: Qubit leakage is a noticeable source of errors for quantum computing. In quantum processors, leakage excitations traveling between qubits generate correlated errors and perturb gate implementations. Leakage mobility can also be utilized for creating dedicated leakage removal pathways and removal units. To quantitatively characterize leakage mobility and to guide better design of processor architectures, we study here leakage dynamics in transmons with tunable couplers through numerical and analytical methods. Even if the couplers are tuned to cancel the single-excitation exchange or the ZZ interaction, the leakage hopping rates still persists in the range of 0.8-10 MHz due to transmon nonlinearity. In typical operation regimes, however, transmon frequency detuning localizes leakage excitations. The next-nearest-neighbor transmons can be still be near-resonant opening leakage tunneling channels. To suppress longer-range hopping, we find that the frequency spread of the next-nearest-neighbor transmons needs to be in the range of 1-4 MHz. Utilizing leakage mobility, we propose two passive leakage removal units. One is based on a tunable coupler and a pumped transmon, and another on a junction readout scheme. Based on realistic experimental parameters, our results on selectively mobilizing or localizing leakage excitations are readily applicable in superconducting quantum devices.

papers.title: A Versatile Analytical Model for Fast and Accurate Determination of Feedline-Coupled Resonators for Superconducting Qubit Readout
papers.abstract: Superconducting quantum chips commonly utilize quarter-wavelength (λ/4) transmission line resonators as readout circuits. An analytical model for the accurate determination of resonance frequencies and coupling Q-factors of feedline-coupled superconducting resonators is introduced. The model leverages four-port microwave network analysis, integrating boundary conditions and conformal mapping techniques to compute even- and odd-mode impedances in edge-coupled coplanar waveguide (CPW) structures. Its versatility allows application to both planar and 3-D heterogeneous architectures, making it a powerful tool for resonator design. To validate the model, a test chip with λ/4 resonators of varying geometries is fabricated and measured in a cryogenic environment. Comparisons with finite element method (FEM) simulations and experimental measurements confirm the model's accuracy, with resonance frequencies and coupling Q-factors aligning closely across configurations. This proposed model facilitates the design of superconducting resonators in readout circuits for more effective, scalable, and adaptable quantum computing architectures.

papers.title: Surface Platinum Alloying for Passivation of Oxide Interfaces on Superconducting Niobium Films
papers.abstract: Dielectric loss arising from two-level systems (TLS) at surfaces and interfaces remains a primary limitation to coherence in superconducting transmon qubits. Niobium (Nb), a widely used material in superconducting quantum circuits, readily forms native oxides under ambient conditions, leading to lossy dielectric interfaces that degrade device performance. Here, a robust and scalable fabrication strategy is demonstrated for chemically stabilizing Nb surfaces and mitigating further oxidation, including protection of both surface and sidewall regions. High-purity Nb films were fabricated with bulk-like superconducting transition temperatures ($T_c = 9.30\pm0.10$) K. We demonstrate that a thin Pt encapsulation layer, deposited after native oxide formation, can be transformed via thermal annealing into a Nb-Pt alloy at the surface. Spectroscopic and microscopic analyses confirm the formation of a chemically stable metallic alloy layer and its ability to suppress further oxide growth. Ab initio simulations elucidate the atomic-scale rearrangement and electronic structure evolution associated with Pt incorporation on native niobium oxide, providing insight into the stabilization mechanism of the alloyed surface. This approach offers a materials pathway for engineering chemically robust Nb interfaces, including sidewalls, toward higher-coherence superconducting qubit architectures."

papers.title: Refrigeration of a one-dimensional gas of microwave photons
papers.abstract: We discuss a conceptually simple scheme for cooling a one-dimensional gas of microwave photons in a superconducting transmission line. By shunting one end of the transmission line by a nonlinear Josephson element, we show how a cooling mechanism can be engineered that transfers photons from high- into low-frequency modes, while preserving their total number. We evaluate the resulting nonequilibrium steady state of the photon gas, which arises from a competition between this engineered cooling process and the natural, number nonconserving thermalization with the surrounding bath. Our analysis predicts that for realistic experimental parameters, this mechanism can be used to prepare photonic gases at submillikelvin temperatures, considerably below the typical base temperature of a dilution refrigerator. In addition, the system exhibits a new type of condensation transition that does not occur in the corresponding equilibrium scenario. As an outlook, we discuss potential applications of this cooling approach for quantum simulation schemes with interacting microwave photons.

papers.title: Imaging the Chemical Structure of the Metal-Substrate Interfaces in Tantalum Superconducting Microwave Resonators for Quantum Devices
papers.abstract: Superconducting resonators and qubits have become a promising platform for quantum computation in the past decades; however, fault-tolerant operation of these devices remains out of reach. In addition to sources within the bulk, interfaces in the device induce dielectric losses and host two-level systems (TLS), diminishing single-photon excitation levels and signal coherence [1]. The metal-substrate (MS) interface has been observed to have disproportionately high electric-field participation in microwave circuits, but with no clear mechanism of how it becomes a dominant source of TLS losses [2]. Establishing a correlation between structural features and performance will be key in realizing fault-tolerant quantum information systems, but atomic-scale characterization of the structural and chemical identity of the MS interface remains limited, and for Ta-based devices, is almost entirely absent. This study presents the use of scanning transmission electron microscopy with electron energy loss spectroscopy (STEM-EELS) of sputtered Ta-on-Si films to investigate roughness and chemical changes of the MS interface when varying substrate deposition temperature and sputtering gas. Deposition conditions ranged between room temperature (RT) and 600 °C using either Kr or Ar gas. In all cases, an amorphous MS interlayer was found. This interlayer grows in thickness progressively with substrate temperature, and at 600 °C, becomes notably thicker in the Ar-sputtered films. The EELS low loss region is difficult to analyze due to overlapping effects from specimen thickness, electron density, and band structure, and discerning subtle changes to core-loss peaks between the metal and substrate is complicated by intermixing from the sputtering process. By using diffusion mapping (DM), individual spectra can be separated by subtle changes in the core-loss [3]. This enables clear distinction between changes in the spectra due to chemical gradients versus silicide formation. Figure 1 shows isolated component regions and spectra for the Si, Ta, and MS interlayer. The change in the Si L2,3 peak shape identifies the formation of a silicide compound at the interface. To corroborate these results, the depth profiles (Figure 2) of Ta and Si for films grown at or above 450° C have a clear shoulder present, also indicating a second interface that may induce its own associated interfacial losses in the device. Superconducting Ta-based resonators and qubits emerged as a promising platform in the quantum information community due to their long coherence times and sub-millisecond relaxation times; however, there is much more progress to be made on identifying and correcting sources of dielectric and TLS loss [1, 4]. In Ta-based films in particular, imaging of interfacial chemical structure has seen little research between the film and substrate, with more attention having instead been devoted to the oxide species at the metal-air interface [5]. This work expands the community’s understanding of where dielectric losses and two-level system behavior may arise in Ta films and highlights how EELS and DM can be leveraged in quantum information research [6]. EELS spectrum images, Si L2, 3 and Ta M5 edge maps, and spectra from Si (blue), interlayer (orange), and Ta (green) regions in the plasmon and Si L2,3, L1 energy ranges for a) RT, b) 450 °C, and c) 600 °C Ar-sputtered films. Scale bar = 5 nm. EELS line profiles across the metal-substrate interface for various 100 nm Ta films.

papers.title: Microwave transmission and dynamical response of three on-chip superconducting resonators coupled to the same molecular spin ensemble
papers.abstract: We study the simultaneous interaction of a sample of organic free radicals, which realize the spin-1/2 model with a quasi-isotropic g factor ≈ 2, with three ≈ 5.5 GHz lumped-element superconducting resonators in a chip. Each resonator consists of a finger capacitor in parallel with a single wire inductor, which maximizes the coupling intensity of the spins to the photon magnetic field. Their frequencies have been detuned relative to one another in order to make them individually addressable. Each resonator within the trio is capacitively coupled to its nearest neighbor and inductively coupled to a common readout transmission line, and only the central one hosts a molecular deposit. The device has been characterized by microwave transmission experiments performed as a function of frequency (between 5.3 and 5.7 GHz) and magnetic field (170–220 mT) at very low temperatures (T ≃ 13 mK). The results evidence a strong local interaction of the spins to the central resonator, which reaches the coherent coupling regime. In addition, they show that the same spins also couple to the modes associated with the distant resonators. These data have been analyzed on the basis of a theoretical model that incorporates the direct spin-photon interactions as well as those mediated by the circuit. The results provide a relatively simple, practical method for investigating spin resonance of a material at multiple frequencies. Besides, this method allows designing each resonator differently, to fulfill a specific role, e.g., for optimized control or readout of the spin states, which can be of relevance for the implementation of hybrid quantum computation schemes based on molecular spin qubits.

papers.title: Quantum Stirling heat machine using two coupled superconducting charge qubits
Robust microwave-to-optical single-photon conversion with a Rydberg atom
papers.abstract: Abstract We propose an efficient scheme for microwave-to-optical quantum frequency conversion mediated by a single atom simultaneously coupled to a superconducting microwave resonator and an optical cavity. The atom mediates efficient interactions between the two electromagnetic modes via non-linear frequency mixing owing to the presence of huge microwave transition dipole moments between nearby Rydberg states as well as suitable optical transitions between low-lying states. In the regime of four-wave mixing with off-resonant fields, the excited states can be adiabatically eliminated, leading to an effective Hamiltonian that directly describes the two-mode interaction responsible for the frequency conversion. However, in this regime, the converter is slow, hence sensitive to losses due to cavity decays. To enhance the performance of the conversion process, we employ pulse engineering to tailor the atom-field couplings. The resulting protocol exhibits high robustness against decoherence and parameter fluctuations, making it well suited for realistic experimental implementations. Our scheme provides a promising route toward high-fidelity and scalable hybrid quantum interfaces connecting superconducting and optical quantum networks.

papers.title: Fast charging of a superconducting qutrit battery via shortcuts to adiabaticity
papers.abstract: Abstract Quantum battery charging in an optimized manner is of significance to quantum state engineering and technology. This paper presents an efficient scheme for rapidly charging a superconducting qutrit battery via shortcuts to adiabaticity. A qutrit battery of superconducting quantum circuit having sufficient level anharmonicity is driven by two classical microwave fields, constituting an effective $\Lambda$-configuration interaction. Within the framework of invariant-based inverse engineering, the fast charging of the qutrit battery can be realized through suitably designing the Rabi frequencies without the restriction of adiabatic criterion. Numerical simulations showcase that the high-efficiency charging could be obtained in the presence of noise decoherence and timing error. Thus the scheme could&#xD;pave a feasible avenue to investigate qutrit battery charging in a fast and robust way in experiments.

papers.title: Canonical quantization of cylindrical waveguides: a gauge-based approach
papers.abstract: Abstract We present a canonical quantization of electromagnetic modes in cylindrical waveguides, extending a gauge-based formalism previously developed for Cartesian geometries (Collin and Delattre 2025 New J. Phys. 27 093502). By introducing the two field quadratures <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi>X</mml:mi> <mml:mo>,</mml:mo> <mml:mi>Y</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> of transverse electric–magnetic, but also of TM (transverse magnetic) and TE (transverse electric) traveling modes, we identify for each a characteristic one-dimensional scalar field (a generalized flux <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi>φ</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> ) governed by a Klein–Gordon type equation. The associated Hamiltonian is derived explicitly from Maxwell’s equations, allowing the construction of bosonic ladder operators. The generalized flux is directly deduced from the electromagnetic potentials <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi mathvariant="bold">A</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> <mml:mo>,</mml:mo> <mml:mi>V</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> by a proper gauge choice , generalizing Devoret’s approach (Devoret 1997 Les Houches, Session LXIII). Our analysis unifies the treatment of cylindrical and Cartesian guided modes under a consistent and generic framework, ensuring both theoretical insight and experimental relevance. Especially, we find out that TE <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:msub> <mml:mrow/> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi>n</mml:mi> <mml:mo>=</mml:mo> <mml:mn>0</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:msub> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> modes break a fundamental gauge symmetry that is observed by all other families. We derive mode-specific capacitance and inductance from the field profiles and express voltage and current in terms of the canonical field variables. Measurable quantities are therefore properly defined from the mode quantum operators, especially for the non-trivial TM and TE ones. The formalism shall extend in future works to any other type of waveguides, especially on-chip coplanar geometries particularly relevant to quantum technologies.

papers.title: Decoherence in waveguide quantum electrodynamics using matrix product states
papers.abstract: We present a matrix product state (MPS) method for including decoherence processes in calculations involving waveguide quantum electrodynamics (QED) using density matrices. The approach is based on collision quantum optics, where the many-body state of the waveguide is represented using discrete time bins, which are then efficiently encoded using an MPS chain. Our method is a generalization of previous MPS methods, and we demonstrate how one can efficiently extend the method to density matrices, allowing for the inclusion of various loss processes in the form of Lindblad terms in the Liouvillian superoperator responsible for the relevant dissipation dynamics. As an application of the theory, we study various waveguide QED systems and the influence of emitter pure dephasing (which is one of the most important processes in real systems) on the light-matter interactions, including a two-level system (TLS) in a semi-infinite waveguide with time-delayed feedback, two spatially separated TLSs with finite delays, and finally the scattering of few-photon Fock pulses on a TLS. In addition to emitter pure dephasing, we also show how to include off-chip radiative decay, and show how it differs qualitatively from pure dephasing.

papers.title: Hadamard random forest for reconstructing real valued pure quantum states
papers.abstract: Many potential quantum computing applications, such as linear system solvers, require efficient readout to preserve the algorithmic speedup, but only involve real amplitudes. Conventional tomography methods demand exponential resources for general complex-valued states. We introduce a readout method for real-valued pure quantum states based on amplitude superposition with Hadamard operations and a random forest algorithm for sign determination. Our method reduces the measurement settings required for state vector reconstruction to $${{{\mathcal{O}}}}({N}_{{{{\rm{q}}}}})$$ for an Nq qubit system; the post-processing cost remains exponential $$\Omega ({2}^{{N}_{{{{\rm{q}}}}}})$$. We experimentally validate our method on up to 10 qubits using the latest available IBM quantum processor and demonstrate that it accurately extracts key properties, such as magic. Our method also outperforms the standard SWAP test for state overlap estimation. This calculation resembles numerical integration in certain cases and can be applied to extract nonlinear properties, which are important in application fields. We further implement the method to read out the solution from a quantum linear solver. Quantum computing applications and system characterization often require efficient state reconstruction, yet conventional methods demand extensive resources. Here, the authors introduce a readout method for real-valued quantum states, significantly reducing measurement settings and outperforming existing techniques like compressed sensing tomography, with implications for enhancing quantum linear solvers and nonlinear property extraction.

papers.title: Alternating Bias Assisted Annealing Influences Amorphous Alumina Structure in Superconducting Quantum Resonators
papers.abstract: Superconducting qubits (SQ) are favorable technology for quantum computing due to their macroscopic nature, coherence times, and gate speeds [1]. Materials synthesis and processing methods for SQs are common to fabrication in the semiconductor industry, promising easy scalability. Josephson junctions (JJ) are critical components of SQs and consist of a thin dielectric layered between two superconducting electrodes [2]. The prototypical JJ is an Al/AlOx/Al sandwich structure, as aluminum forms a thin, self-limiting oxide [2, 3]. Amorphous alumina (a-AlOx) has also seen widespread adoption as a dielectric in semiconducting devices due to favorable properties such as high breakdown fields and low leakage currents [4]. Aluminum oxidation follows Cabrera-Mott (CM) mechanisms, where adatom-induced fields drive Al-ion diffusion towards the surface [3]. Pappas et al. introduced alternating bias assisted annealing (ABAA), an electrical processing technique to tune JJ resistance [5]. ABAA applies alternating voltage pulses, below the JJ breakdown field but above the CM field, hypothesized to facilitate ionic diffusion and anneal the oxide. Via scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), they demonstrated that ABAA induces a measurable change on the Al electron energy loss near-edge structure (EELS-ELNES), suggestive of potential changes in bonding and homogenization of the oxide [5]. Junction resistance with ABAA can be tuned to a narrow distribution, improving device performance [6]. Iaia et al. studied the influence of ABAA in thicker a-AlOx layers in superconducting resonators designed to study two level system defects (TLS) in the amorphous dielectric [7]. They note pronounced impact of ABAA applied and measured at mK temperatures (cryogenic alternating bias stimulation, CABS) on TLS behavior, which are reversible when the device is annealed to 10 K. In this work, we investigate the influence of ABAA on a-AlOx film structure using 4D STEM fluctuation electron microscopy (FEM). Synthesis and processing of the device is described in Iaia et al. [7]. Briefly, a ∼50 nm thick a-AlOx layer was synthesized via thermal atomic layer deposition (ALD), which differs from conventional a-AlOx growth in JJs. ABAA processing was applied with ±100 MV/m fields at 353 K over 30 hours. STEM sample thickness was controlled between 0.4 – 0.7 λEMFPAlOx⁠. 4D STEM experiments were performed at 300 kV on the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory TEAM I, collected with a Dectris Arina detector, with a 1.2 mrad and 2 pA probe to minimize beam damage [8]. Thickness was calculated for each real space position based on the transmitted intensity of the diffraction zero-beam using a vacuum dataset for reference. The variance was normalized for thickness at each pixel and averaged across each row of diffraction patterns. Several datasets were collected, aligned, normalized, and averaged to improve statistics. Variance profiles are compared as a function of depth to understand a-AlOx medium range order across the device thickness. Figure 1 shows FEM analysis of a resonator. Fluctuation electron microscopy (FEM) variance was calculated using the Vr method for each pixel [9]. Variance is a metric which tracks how speckle intensity as a function of k fluctuates across a dataset [10]. Speckles originate from individual ordered atomic clusters in the amorphous material aligned on Bragg conditions [10]. A low variance is suggestive of a lower speckle-contrast amorphous halo with little fluctuation across the dataset, or a more uniform and amorphous structure. In contrast, a higher variance suggests stronger speckle contrast intensity fluctuations, with sources arising from both discrete speckles and changes across the dataset, or a more heterogeneous and ordered amorphous material. Figure 1 compares FEM normalized variance profiles between the as-made (AM) and ABAA devices, and Figure 2 isolates the peak variance values at ∼3 and ∼7 nm-1 as a function of distance from the TiN electrode. In the AM device, a pronounced decrease in the variance is observed near the TiN interface, suggesting a substantial reduction in amorphous structural order. This variance reduction extends several nm into the film. We speculate this may be attributable to TiN interfacial effects during the initial stages of the ALD growth. Datasets collected with different cross-sections, probe currents, shorter dwell times, and different scan geometries all show comparable TiN interfacial features, so we believe this effect is not attributable to electron or ion beam damage [8]. The ABAA-treated device shows only a modest variance reduction near the TiN interface. This suggests that ABAA increases the a-AlOx ordering near the interface. While the a-AlOx structure as a function of depth is more homogeneous after ABAA, the a-AlOx structure near the TiN interface can be thought of as more heterogeneous, peppered with well-ordered atomic clusters. We interpret this change as ABAA-induced ionic diffusion allowing the oxide to find more stable configurations [4,5]. ABAA thus offers a straightforward means to modify both the structure and properties of ALD AlOx layers inside devices [11]. Overview of spatially-resolved FEM measurements. A 4D STEM dataset is depicted by a virtual brightfield (vBF) image (top left). Each diffraction pattern’s variance is calculated, normalized based on the pixel thickness, and averaged across each row. Variances are compared as a function of depth in the AlOx layer. A representative diffraction pattern is shown (top right), with rings corresponding to maxima in the variance. Spatially resolved, normalized variance plots are shown for the as-made (bottom left) and ABAA (bottom right) devices with colors corresponding to locations depicted by the vBF colorbar. FEM comparisons between AM and ABAA devices. The AM device shows reduced variance near the TiN interface, mostly mitigated via ABAA processing.

papers.title: Fluctuation-Cepstral Analysis of Structural Heterogeneity in Al/AlOx/Al Josephson Junctions
papers.abstract: The Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junction (JJ) is a ubiquitous component across most superconducting qubit architectures for quantum technologies [1]. In these structures, defects within the ultrathin (∼2 nm) AlOx barrier are thought to generate two-level systems (TLSs) that couple strongly to the qubit, reducing their coherence time and reliability [2]. Correspondingly, understanding the atomic-scale origins of TLS is a critical challenge for advancing quantum computing. Despite the importance of the AlOx layer, it remains difficult to probe its structure due to its amorphous nature and nanometer-scale dimensions. In this work, we use 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) to establish an analysis framework for resolving hidden structural heterogeneity in the AlOx barrier. Unlike real-space imaging methods, nanodiffraction is highly sensitive to changes in atomic ordering in amorphous materials [3]. In particular, the cepstrum, the inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) of the log of the diffraction intensity, enables the detection of subtle, periodic correlations within the amorphous material [4]. Using fluctuation-cepstral scanning transmission electron microscopy (FC-STEM) [4], we show that, rather than being uniform, the ordering of AlOx layer varies with the local Al grain structure. Moreover, we demonstrate the application of FC-STEM for measuring the structure of amorphous oxide thin films and understanding the microscopic origins of defects in quantum computers. Figure 1a shows a high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) STEM image of a JJ with electrodes composed of relatively large (100–150 nm) grains, and Figure 1b presents a magnified atomic-resolution image of the AlOx layer and its interfaces with the Al electrodes. Figure 1c demonstrates that the TLS density decreases with decreasing grain boundary density, indicating that TLS density is correlated to the electrode structure and local microstructural environment of the junction. To understand the origins of these correlations, we conducted FC-STEM to study the local order of the Al/ AlOx interface. Figure 2a shows a virtual 4D-STEM image of a JJ device, where the red region indicates the area selected for analysis. Figures 2b and 2c display 4D-STEM stacks and their corresponding cepstrum images obtained at individual scan pixels. To selectively evaluate fluctuations within a targeted structural length-scale range, we select specific inner and outer radii (r_in and r_out) in the cepstral annulus, as indicated by the red circle in Figure 2c and the values in parentheses in Figure 2d. As shown in Figure 2d (i) and (ii), regions of high fluctuation extend beyond the oxide layer, and the magnitude of fluctuation within the oxide varies across grain boundaries in the bottom electrode. Finally, Figure 2d (iii) demonstrates that the grain-dependent fluctuation varies significantly with the selected periodicity range, providing insight into which structural length scales contribute most strongly to structural heterogeneity in the JJ [5]. Correlation between TLS density and junction microstructure. (a) Representative cross-sectional high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF)-STEM images of JJ with low grain boundary density. (b) Atomic-resolution image of the Al/AlOx/Al junction. (c) TLS density measured for devices with high grain boundary density (green) and low grain boundary density (yellow). Fluctuation-cepstral analysis of the JJ structure. (a) A virtual 4D-STEM image of JJ, with red boxes indicating individual scan points within the region of interest. (b) Stacked 4D-STEM patterns and (c) corresponding cepstrum images for each scan point, where the red annulus denotes the target inner and outer radii (r_in and r_out) for fluctuation analysis. (d) FC-STEM map calculated from the cepstrum stacks. (i) Virtual 4D-STEM image of the bottom electrode exhibiting two distinct grain orientations. (ii) FC-STEM of (i) calculated within the target annulus (r_in, r_out) = (1.54, 4.26) Å. The arrow highlights the extended fluctuation from the oxide into the electrode interface, and a clear difference in oxide fluctuation between the two grains is observed. (iii) FC-STEM maps calculated in annular ranges of (1.57, 2.24), (2.24, 2.91), (2.91, 3.58), and (3.58, 4.26).

papers.title: Near-single-domain superconducting aluminium films on GaAs(111)A with remarkable crystalline quality for scalable quantum circuits
papers.abstract: The realization of highly coherent and scalable superconducting quantum circuits relies critically on the structural perfection of epitaxial aluminium (Al) films. However, the presence of twin boundaries in these materials introduces prominent decoherence channels that severely limit device performance. Here, we have reproducibly grown near-single-domain superconducting Al films on GaAs(111)A wafers using molecular beam epitaxy. Synchrotron X-ray diffraction revealed twin-domain ratios of 0.00005 and 0.0003 for 19.4-nm- and 9.6-nm-thick films, respectively—the lowest reported for Al on any substrate and long considered unattainable for practical device platforms. Azimuthal scans across off-normal Al{$$11\bar{1}$$} reflections exhibit narrow full width at half maximum (FWHM) values down to 0.55°, unmatched by epi-Al grown by any other method. Normal scans showed a well-defined (111) orientation with pronounced Pendellösung fringes, and θ-rocking-curve FWHM values down to 0.018°; the former indicates abrupt film–substrate and oxide–film interfaces. Electron backscatter diffraction mapping confirms macroscopic in-plane uniformity and the absence of Σ3 twin domains. Atomic force microscopy and scanning transmission electron microscopy confirmed atomically smooth surfaces and abrupt heterointerfaces. The films exhibit critical temperatures approaching bulk values, establishing a materials platform for scalable, high-coherence superconducting qubits. The structural perfection of epitaxial aluminium films is crucial for advancing superconducting quantum circuits, yet twin boundaries hinder device performance. Here, the authors achieve near-single-domain superconducting Al films on Ga-terminated GaAs(111) wafers, demonstrating ultralow twin-domain ratios, atomically smooth surfaces, and abrupt heterointerfaces, paving the way for scalable, high-performance quantum devices.

papers.title: Characterization of Tantalum and Tantalum-alloyed Films for Quantum Devices
papers.abstract: Superconducting qubits are among the most advanced platforms for quantum information, offering potential scalability and compatibility with standard device fabrication techniques [1-5]. Among the materials investigated for superconducting qubits, Tantalum (Ta) has emerged as a compelling candidate due to its self-terminating stoichiometric surface oxide and chemical resistance to harsh post-fabrication processes. Efforts to mitigate surface loss by treating the surface oxides and utilizing high-resistivity silicon substrates have led to Ta-based qubits with lifetime and coherence times exceeding 1 ms [3]. Guided by these successes in reducing dielectric loss in Ta-based devices, we are interested in exploring material engineering approaches that enhance the superconducting gap. Alloying Ta with another element to enhance the superconducting performance expands the range of viable material candidates available to tackle different loss channels in superconducting circuits [1]. Recently, we explore superconducting gap engineering in Ta-based devices as a powerful strategy for expanding the range of suitable host materials. By alloying 20 at.% hafnium (Hf) into Ta thin films, we achieve a superconducting transition temperature (Tc) of 6.09 K as observed in direct current (DC) transport measurements, reflecting an increase in the superconducting gap. Here we demonstrate an approach for controlling varying deposition conditions to control film orientation and transport properties of Ta and Ta-Hf alloy thin films. We investigate the microstructure and composition distribution of the thin films by using high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) with super-X EDS system (no serious beam damage issue [6-8]). Our structural analysis using TEM diffraction and STEM verifies the BCC structure across all the films (Figure 1), and direct current (DC) transport measurements reveal a 40% enhancement in Tc relative to undoped Ta (Tc=4.3 K). We monitored oxide growth over an 18-day period following film deposition to better understand how Hf incorporation influences surface oxides. In both Ta and Hf spectra, the fraction of fully oxidized (Ta2O5 and HfO2) states gradually increased during the 18-day exposure, indicating progressive surface oxidation. To estimate the surface oxide thickness, we use cross-sectional TEM/EDS mapping (Figure 1c). The analysis reveals that the oxide thickness for the 1 ks Ta-Hf alloy film is approximately 3 nm in thickness, comparable to the 3 nm oxide observed on native Ta [2]. For the 2 ks Ta-Hf film, the oxide thickness increases slightly to about 4 nm (Figure 1). The measured surface loss tangent of the Ta-Hf alloy remains comparable to that of native Ta. This result suggests that the surface oxide of the Ta-Hf alloy, which contains a measurable fraction of HfOx, does not introduce additional dielectric loss. By engineering the alloy composition and film deposition, this study achieves both improved superconducting properties and compatibility with fabrication processes. These findings show that material doping and alloying can strategically expand the suite of viable materials for superconducting quantum devices. This approach provides a pathway for tailoring material properties to support the next generation of quantum technologies and offers broad relevance to researchers in materials science, quantum information, and device engineering [9]. STEM images on cross sections of 1 ks (a) and 2 ks (b) Ta-Hf thin films, both films were sputtered at 750 ◦C. (c) Cross-sectional EDS elemental mapping on Ta-Hf. Cross-sectional EDS mapping Ta (blue) and Hf (orange) confirmed a uniform Ta-Hf alloy with the Ta to Hf atomic ratios for the bulk to be (83% : 17%). The oxygen (red) map reveals a surface oxide layer with the estimated surface oxide thickness of around 4 nm. The 1 ks Ta-Hf film exhibits an oxide thickness of approximately 3 nm, similar to that of native Ta. The EDS resolution limit is 0.5 atomic percent.

papers.title: 3D Atomic-Scale Characterization of Defects in Superconducting TiN Resonator with Multislice Electron Ptychography
papers.abstract: Characterizing the microscopic sources of loss are becoming increasingly critical for the development of stable superconducting qubits. Commons sources of loss reside at material interfaces where nanoscale defects such as vacancies, impurities, undesirable oxides, and dislocations occur [1]. However, it is challenging to characterize defects that occur inside materials and devices - e.g., expitaxial thin film TiN on sapphire substrate used to create superconducting qubits - with common imaging methods like annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (ADF-STEM) due to challenge of separating surface from interior defects in projection and lack of sensitivity to lighter elements like oxygen and nitrogen in the presence of relatively heavier elements like titanium (Figure 1a). The artifacts associated with multiple scattering of the beam in the sample pose difficulties in analysis due to the breakdown of linear imaging theory [2]. Under these circumstances, multislice electron ptychography (MEP) is well-adapted to image the full atomic structure required for individual defect analysis while explicitly addressing multiple scattering effects [3]. Since the phase of the electron wave is reconstructed at each slice of the sample along the depth direction, 3D information about the atomic potentials can be extracted. This is particularly advantageous as many crystalline defects and dislocation manifest as 3D structures. Figures 1b-f show the depth slices of a single screw dislocation in a sample of TiN on sapphire ∼40 nm-thick along the beam (depth) direction. A 3D visualization of various atomic-scale dislocations is shown in Figure 2. Individual edge dislocations associated with lattice mismatch between TiN and sapphire (i.e. misfit dislocations) and threading dislocation in TiN are mapped, as well as screw dislocation. Despite the periodic array of the misfit dislocations indicating a fully relaxed film, potentially lossy threading and screw dislocations persist [4]. Interface of expitaxial TiN on sapphire substrate. (a) HAADF-STEM image of misoriented grains in projection resulting in blurry atoms in TiN. (b) - (f) These are cleanly resolved by multislice electron ptychography (MEP) depth-sections from a single reconstruction at various z-depths in the sample ((b) z = 24.2 nm, (c) z = 26.4 nm, (d) z = 27.5 nm, (e) z = 28.6 nm, (f) z = 29.7 nm) showing the screw component of a dislocation between two grains. A 3D visualization of dislocation networks connected to the TiN on sapphire interface. Identified defects are labeled in (a) and (b): 1 - misfit dislocations along the interface occur in generally periodic array due to ∼7.5% lattice mismatch between TiN and sapphire; 2 - threading dislocation in TiN correlated to a discontinuity in misfit dislocation; 3 - screw dislocation. Interface is outlined by dashed line and lateral field-of-view along x-direction is 15.2 nm. Due to the finite depth resolution, defect markers are interpolated along z between each MEP slices, each which are 0.85 nm thick.

papers.title: Candidate TLS Defects at the Al-Si Interface in a Superconducting Qubit from STEM-based Structure Refinement
papers.abstract: Two-level systems (TLSs) are the dominant source of decoherence in superconducting qubits, a leading platform for quantum computing. While TLSs are believed to arise from atomic-scale tunneling defects, their precise structural origins, particularly at complex and disordered interfaces in real devices, have remained elusive. Conventional structural characterization is extremely challenging because these interfaces are non-periodic, containing steps and roughness, and device-relevant TLS defects involve only atomic motions with small energy differences. We have determined the atomic character of candidate TLSs at the Al-Si interface of a superconducting qubit using aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) combined with experiment-constrained 3D structure modeling and computational defect searching. High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) STEM images were obtained from a disordered interface containing a prominent step defect and localized strain. Structure modeling started with 3D models created in the Ingrained framework to match the experimental projections, accounting for mistilt and uniform strain. These models were then refined using FANTASTX (Fully Automated Nanoscale To Atomistic Structure from Theory and eXperiments), a multi-objective optimizer that simultaneously minimizes disagreement with the experimental image via structural similarity and the ab initio (DFT) total system energy. Transition-state searches with the activation relaxation technique nouveau (ARTn) on the refined models identified many atomic configurations occupying double-well potentials corresponding to TLS. Statistical analysis of over 1500 TLSs shows that candidate TLS with tunneling energies and asymmetries in the range relevant to superconducting qubits (∼5 GHz) predominantly involve Al atoms located near the interface. These atoms exhibit smaller median tunneling displacements (∼0.44 Å) than the non-candidate TLS and reside in locally disordered environments with marginally longer and less dense first-neighbor shells than those of non-candidate TLSs. The most probable candidate TLSs feature cooperative motion of one or two Al atoms, and sometimes with Si, in directions largely parallel to the interface. This work provides the first direct atomic-scale insight into the structural defects that may be responsible for decoherence at a realistic, device-relevant interface. It also demonstrates a scalable, generalizable workflow for solving the atomic structure of complex, disordered interfaces by integrating aberration-corrected STEM with advanced computational refinement and defect searching. The methodology is directly applicable to other materials systems and heterointerfaces critical to quantum devices [5].

papers.title: Correlative Reciprocal-Space and Spectral Mapping of the Quantum Microstructure in High-Performance Epitaxial Materials for Superconducting Qubits
papers.abstract: Superconducting qubit technology is among the most promising hardware platform for quantum computing due to its fast gate operation, manufacturing scalability, and architectural flexibility [1]. A key figure of merit that dictates quantum computing functionality is the qubit’s coherence time, which needs to be maximized in order to bring quantum computing to the practical and scalable realm [2]. In particular, the T1 relaxation time—now on the order of milliseconds—can be enhanced with materials engineering, as amorphous dielectrics and crystallographic defects, among other factors, are known to induce decoherence [3-7]. Current state-of-the-art superconducting qubit devices use amorphous AlOx sandwiched between two superconducting Al electrodes as the Josephson junction (JJ), a key element in the transmon qubit, but amorphous dielectrics introduce two-level system (TLS) loss that underlie decoherence [8]. For this reason, numerous efforts have explored crystalline dielectrics as a replacement for amorphous AlOx, since single-crystal materials do not suffer from the lack of long-range order and sub-stoichiometry that comprise TLS defects [9-12]. However, none of these alternative materials choices have been able to surpass, let alone replicate, the performance of Al-AlOx-Al JJs. In this work, we fabricate superconducting quantum devices using a novel heteroepitaxial TiN/γ-Al2O3/TiN tri-layer stack grown on sapphire (Fig. 1a) and find that the measured microwave loss of the single-crystal γ-Al2O3 dielectric is lower than that of amorphous AlOx by two orders of magnitude. For qubits made with this tri-layer to transcend the coherence of incumbent Al-AlOx-Al, the structural, chemical, and electronic defects that induce TLS loss in these materials need to be well understood. Towards this end, we combine scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) methods to highlight structural and interfacial complexity across length scales, ultimately identifying loss sources in the TiN/γ-Al2O3/TiN heteroepitaxial tri-layer. With atomic-resolution imaging and four-dimensional (4D-)STEM nanobeam electron diffraction (NBED), we find that the dielectric γ-Al2O3 layer, though single-crystalline (Fig. 1b), suffers from the formation of antiphase boundaries (Fig. 1c), which can host strong local electric fields and enhance lossy dielectric response [13]. Correlated with these nanoscale planar defects is uniformly distributed elastic strain, on the order of 6%, between the lattice-mismatched γ-Al2O3 and TiN (Fig. 1d). In other words, the dielectric layer is fully strained to match the underlying metal layer; such high strain can distort local bonding environments and thus create new TLSs or shift existing TLSs into resonance. Beyond imperfections within the bulk of the dielectric layer, there are noteworthy interfacial defects: roughening of both TiN/γ-Al2O3 interfaces deviate from atomically flat boundaries (Fig. 1c), while anion interdiffusion across both interfaces, as evident from core-loss electron energy-loss spectral (EELS) maps (Fig. 1e), leave behind vacancies and undercoordinated metal atoms, thereby creating 1.5 – 2 nm nonstoichiometric diffuse interfacial layers, both of which can cause TLS loss. In the superconducting TiN layers, we again use NBED to identify 180°-reflected specular twinned domains, indicating distinct heteroepitaxial relationships of [111]TiN//[0006]Al2O3 and [002¯]TiN//[22¯02¯]Al2O3 (Fig. 2a) [14]. Crystal twinning of the TiN epilayer is not only spatially distributed at the nanoscale, as shown using virtual dark-field (VDF) images (Fig. 2b), but is also widespread at the microscale, as shown using SEM electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) (Fig. 2c). While microwave performance is not limited by a single factor, it is clear that defective quantum microstructure across length scales collectively contribute to dielectric loss, and in turn, TLS-related decoherence. By correlating nanoscale crystallographic and spectroscopic information with microscale diffraction measurements, our work can guide interface engineering during material growth, paving the way towards further improvements in quantum device performance. Cross-sectional samples were prepared by subsequent 30 kV, 8 kV and 5 kV Xe+ plasma focused ion beam (FIB) using the Thermo Scientific Helios 5 Hydra CX DualBeam Plasma FIB/SEM. Samples were then plasma cleaned using South Bay Technology PC-2000 Plasma Cleaner with a 3:1 mixture of Ar:O2 gas at 20∼40 W RF power for 15 s at 150 mTorr. High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF-) and annular bright-field (ABF-) STEM images were collected on a probe-corrected JEOL JEM-ARM200CF S/TEM operating at 200 kV using JEOL detectors. The STEM convergence angle, HAADF collection angle, and ABF collection angle were 27 mrad, 90 – 370 mrad, and 23 mrad, respectively. EELS data were collected on a JEOL JEM-ARM300F GrandARM S/TEM operating at 300 kV using the Gatan GIF Continuum K3 IS system. The data were collected using a 2.5 mm aperture and a 750 eV wide energy slit at a dispersion of 0.18 eV/Ch and a camera length of 2 cm. 4D-STEM data were collected on the same microscope and detector system using a 0.5 – 1.5 mrad convergence angle and a 20 eV wide energy slit at a camera length of 4 cm. All STEM data processing was performed using the Gatan Microscopy Suite software. Top-down EBSD measurements were performed in the Thermo Scientific Helios 5 CX DualBeam FIB/SEM at 25 kV using the Oxford Symmetry S3 detector. EBSD data processing was performed using the Oxford AZtecCrystal software [15]. Defects in γ-Al2O3. a) HAADF-STEM image of a TiN/γ-Al2O3/TiN tri-layer stack on a α-Al2O3 (0001) substrate. The thickness of γ-Al2O3 is approximately 13.5 nm. b) 4D-STEM NBED pattern of the γ-Al2O3 layer, confirming the {111} out-of-plane orientation. c) Fourier-filtered atomic-resolution ABF-STEM image of the γ-Al2O3 dielectric layer, taken from the cyan-colored square region in a), emphasizing the planar defects along both TiN/γ-Al2O3 interfaces and within the γ-Al2O3 layer itself–interfacial roughness (yellow lines) and antiphase boundaries (colored parallelograms), respectively. The scale bar is 2 nm. d) In-plane and out-of-plane strain maps of the heteroepitaxial tri-layer stack, with approximately 6.5∼6.8% strain in both directions. The units of the intensity bar are such that 100% strain would be equivalent to 1.0. e) STEM-EELS maps of Ti-L2,3, N-K, and O-K edges, along with a superimposed image of the three, taken from the same region as c). The scale bars are all 5 nm. Defects in TiN. a) 4D-STEM NBED patterns and b) VDF images of nanoscale TiN {111} and {002} twins. c) SEM EBSD pole figures in the three face-centered cubic crystallographic directions, revealing that the 60° rotation twinning behavior (with the [111] twin axis) is spread across the microscale.

papers.title: Multi-Modal Atomic-Scale Characterization of Interfacial Defects in Superconducting Transmon Qubits
papers.abstract: In superconducting transmon qubits, macroscopic characterization is the primary method for probing performance metrics, such as relaxation T1 and dephasing T2 times, resonance frequency, and quality factor. While these measurements can aid our understanding of the dielectric loss of a transmon, they do not allow us to characterize the structural and chemical inhomogeneity of the interfaces which directly impacts this energy loss. These fundamental materials problems must be studied using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to provide insight into these defects across different qubit interfaces at an atomic scale. In this contribution, we will examine qubits, such as those shown in Figure 1, fabricated at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (SQMS Center) [1]. The qubit devices consist of superconducting metal base layers, typically sputter deposited Nb or Ta, and Al/AlOx/Al junctions, where the AlOx barrier is roughly 3nm in thickness and prepared through in-situ oxidation [2]. Characterizing this system prior to its integration within a superconducting radio frequency cavity establishes a baseline for the system, allowing us to isolate fabrication-induced defects before they manifest in performance degradation during quantum measurements. With the samples and fabrication process well known on a macroscopic scale, we study the atomic structure and chemistry of different heterointerfaces within the Josephson junction (JJ) of the transmon qubit and between the sapphire substrate and Nb resonator pads to identify potential defects contributing to the decoherence for qubits constructed with particular geometries. To resolve these defects, atomic-resolution imaging, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and electron-energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) are performed using the JEOL-ARM200CF, an aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM). Figure 2 provides a clear image of the stacked layers formed as the JJ, but with the addition of a platinum and carbon protective coating added during the focus ion beam (FIB) milling process to preserve pristine Al/AlOx/Al interfaces. 4D-STEM approaches, such as ptychography, orientation mapping and nanoscale diffraction will be employed to further study the layered interfaces and defects in real space and reciprocal space. These techniques can also provide insight into any damage that incurs during lamella preparation using the FIB [3]. Magnetic field-free atomic resolution imaging, differential phase contrast mapping, and monochromated EELS can be achieved using the new MARS-MONO STEM (JEM-Z200MF) without inducing current fluctuations or magnetic field related distortions [4]. By integrating this work across the functional interfaces of the transmon qubits and their different geometries, we will identify possible structural and chemical defects which limit device performance using our multi-modal approach [5]. SQMS fabricated transmon qubits fabricated on HEMEX sapphire substrate imaged via a) ZEISS optical microscope, b) SEM and c) EDS. TEM image of Josephson Junction layered interface at on JEOL-ARM200CF on the ClearView camera with a 200kV accelerating voltage.

papers.title: Control of Qubit–Qubit Coupling with Double Superconducting Resonators
papers.abstract: We experimentally studied the switching off processes in the double-resonator coupler superconducting quantum circuit. In both frequency and time-domain, we observed the variation of qubit-qubit effective coupling by tuning the frequency differences between qubits and the double-resonator coupler. According to the measurement results, by just shifting about 50 MHz of qubits' frequencies, we can tune the effective qubit-qubit coupling strength from switching off point to two qubit gate point (effective coupling larger than 5 MHz) in double-resonator superconducting quantum circuit.The double-resonator (coupler) superconducting quantum circuit has the advantage of simple fabrications, introducing less flux noises, reducing occupancy of dilution refrigerator cables,which might supply a promising platform for future large-scale superconducting quantum processors.
papers.journal: Journal of the Physical Society of Japan

papers.title: Exploring Three‐Photon Resonance and Generating Squeezed‐Light Entanglement via Parametric Amplification
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We propose an efficient and robust protocol for the generation of entanglement between a superconducting qubit and a squeezed cavity. By applying a parametric drive to the cavity coupled to the qubit, the dynamical evolution of the system is precisely described by an anisotropic Rabi model within a squeezed reference frame. Utilizing time‐averaging methods, we analytically derive the resonance conditions and the effective Rabi frequency for the high‐order three‐photon process. By implementing an adiabatic passage, slowly tuning the cavity frequency across the resonance, the system is steered into a maximally entangled state, e.g., between the three‐photon state and the qubit excited state in the squeezed picture. Numerical simulations confirm that the target state can be prepared with a population close to 1 under ideal conditions, and even in the presence of realistic environmental noise, an appreciable state fidelity of 0.77 and an entanglement concurrence of 0.71 can still be preserved, demonstrating the high robustness of our protocol. Our method provides a practical pathway for generating complex non‐Gaussian entangled states, which are of significant value for fault‐tolerant quantum computation and quantum metrology beyond the standard quantum limit.

papers.title: Magneto-optical study of Nb thin films for superconducting qubits
papers.abstract: Abstract Among the recognized sources of decoherence in superconducting qubits, the spatial inhomogeneity of the superconducting state and the possible presence of magnetic-flux vortices remain comparatively underexplored. Niobium is commonly used as a structural material in transmon qubits that host Josephson junctions, and excess dissipation anywhere in the transmon can become a bottleneck that limits overall quantum performance. The metal/substrate interfacial layer may simultaneously host pair-breaking loss channels (e.g. two-level systems) and control thermal transport, thereby affecting dissipation and temperature stability. Here, we use quantitative magneto-optical imaging of the magnetic-flux distribution to characterize the homogeneity of the superconducting state and the critical current density, <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:msub> <mml:mi>j</mml:mi> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi mathvariant="normal">c</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> </mml:msub> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> , in niobium films fabricated under different sputtering conditions. The imaging reveals distinct flux-penetration regimes, ranging from a nearly ideal Bean critical state to strongly nonuniform thermo-magnetic dendritic avalanches. By fitting the measured magnetic-induction profiles, we extract <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:msub> <mml:mi>j</mml:mi> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi mathvariant="normal">c</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> </mml:msub> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> and try to correlate it with film physical properties and with measured qubit internal quality factors. Our results indicate that the Nb/Si interlayer can be a significant contributor to decoherence and should be considered an important factor that must be optimized.

papers.title: Transducer leakage error suppression using invariant-based shortcut
papers.abstract: Abstract We present a method for suppressing transducer leakage errors in spin-superconducting hybrid quantum systems with the theory of optimal invariant-based shortcut. By mediated virtual photons as a transducer to exchange the energy between the spin qubit and a transmon qubit, the fidelity of the population of the final state features a broad range above 99% under the influence of leakage error. The leakage probability from computational subspace to non-computational subspace can be effectively suppressed at a lowest value with <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:mn>0.01</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> . Based on the optimized pulse control designed by the invariant-based inverse engineering, the high-fidelity quantum iSWAP gate operations and entanglement state preparation within the computational subspace are achieved. Compared to the traditional <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mml:mrow> <mml:mi>π</mml:mi> </mml:mrow> </mml:math> pulse, derivative removal by adiabatic gate, counter-diabatic shortcut schemes, and limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno gradient ascent pulse engineering, the optimized shortcut scheme can still achieve a high fidelity with 99% in the presence of decoherence and control error. When taking into account the possibility of leakage errors in actual situations, our solution can still largely resist the influence of control errors. The results provides a feasible path for precisely manipulating the quantum state of hybrid quantum systems.

papers.title: Multi-product Zeno effect achieving higher order convergence rates
papers.abstract: The quantum Zeno effect is a fundamental mechanism for implementing the effective dynamics of projected Hamiltonian and Lindbladian systems. It approximates the target projected evolution by interleaving Hamiltonian or Lindblad dynamics with quantum operations associated with the desired subspace. In contrast to the related Trotter product formula, the best-known convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect is typically limited to order <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mml:mn>1</mml:mn> <mml:mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD"> <mml:mo>/</mml:mo> </mml:mrow> <mml:mi>n</mml:mi> </mml:math> . In this work, we improve this convergence rate by employing a multi-product formula, thereby achieving arbitrarily high-order convergence of the form <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mml:mn>1</mml:mn> <mml:mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD"> <mml:mo>/</mml:mo> </mml:mrow> <mml:msup> <mml:mi>n</mml:mi> <mml:mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD"> <mml:mi>K</mml:mi> <mml:mo>+</mml:mo> <mml:mn>1</mml:mn> </mml:mrow> </mml:msup> </mml:math> . This yields an improved approximation scheme for Zeno-like expectation values via an efficient post-processing method. The approach combines a modified Chernoff lemma, an adapted Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation. We illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and also consider the broader class of systems governed by the Bang-Bang decoupling method.

papers.title: A Critical Review of Pulse Tube Cryocooler Technologies and Their Compressor Systems
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Pulse tube cryocoolers (PTCs) are advanced cryogenic refrigeration systems known for high reliability, low vibration, compactness, and absence of moving parts at the cold end. Recent developments in compressor technologies, phase-shift mechanisms, and regenerator optimization have expanded their applications in aerospace, superconducting devices, medical imaging, and quantum technologies. This review critically evaluates recent advancements in pulse tube cryocooler technologies, compressor systems, phase-shift mechanisms, and performance enhancement techniques while identifying research gaps, bottlenecks, and future development opportunities. Method: A systematic review was conducted using peer-reviewed studies from Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and IEEE Xplore databases covering 2020–2026. Relevant studies were selected based on cryogenic performance, compressor technologies, and experimental or numerical validation. Comparative analyses were performed for pulse tube configurations, phase-shift techniques, compressor systems, regenerator materials, and heat exchanger designs using parameters such as cooling temperature, thermodynamic efficiency, cooling capacity, pressure ratio, and vibration characteristics. The findings were synthesized using comparative tables, performance graphs, and critical analytical discussions. Findings: The review revealed that inertance-type and double-inlet pulse tube cryocoolers achieve nearly 15–25% higher thermodynamic efficiency and improved phase synchronization compared with conventional systems. Recent gas-bearing and moving-coil compressors demonstrated approximately 30–40% lower vibration levels and improved operational stability. High-efficiency miniature cryocoolers operating near 150 K achieved cooling capacities above 500 W with reduced acoustic losses. However, thermal leakage, regenerator inefficiency, synchronization instability, and manufacturing complexity remain major bottlenecks. The study further highlights milestone developments and future opportunities involving AI-assisted optimization, advanced regenerator materials, additive manufacturing, and compact low-vibration cryogenic systems. Significance: Unlike earlier reviews focused mainly on thermodynamic descriptions, the present study establishes a comparative framework linking pulse tube configurations, compressor technologies, phase-shift mechanisms, and cryogenic performance. The review uniquely integrates technological advancements, bottlenecks, commercialization challenges, and future research directions within a single comprehensive framework. Keywords: Pulse tube cryocooler, Cryogenic refrigeration, Cam and follower compressor, Phase shift mechanism, Regenerator, Cryocooler performance
papers.journal: Indian Journal of Science and Technology

papers.title: The Energy-Advantage Frontier of Random Circuit Sampling Across the Simulability Transition
papers.abstract: We introduce the energy-advantage frontier of random circuit sampling (RCS)—the locus in the noise-rate/size plane where the classical and quantum energy-to-solution are equal—and locate it relative to the noise-induced classical-simulability transition. Our firm, model-free result is that the classical sampling-energy floor collapses sharply across the transition, exhibiting a finite-size scaling collapse over exact systems n≤12 (with a collapse exponent of order unity). Built on it, the energy-advantage frontier is distinct from the computational (wall-clock) frontier: in the exascale-classical, few-femtojoule regime, the energy frontier is the more noise-robust, so an energy advantage can persist where a time advantage does not—a projection, not a deployment claim, whose direction reverses outside that regime. We give a conditional Landauer lower bound for sampling, RE≡Ecl/Eq≳2(1.0±0.2)n/n under standard RCS hardness, package RE as a single figure of merit computed by a released open tool (exs), and map an energy-normalized cross-entropy witness within a cost model. A run on a 156-qubit IBM Heron processor tests the fidelity model (no energy is measured on hardware) and shows real noise exceeds the depolarizing idealization, so quoted frontier locations are upper bounds.

papers.title: Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization Methods for Modeling the Photochemistry of Diazirine and Diazo Compounds
papers.abstract: Diazirines and diazo compounds are widely employed as photoreactive precursors for generating carbenes, key intermediates in chemical biology and materials science. However, computationally modeling their reaction pathways remains challenging due to the need for large active spaces and the requirement to accurately capture excited-state surfaces along with transition states and conical intersections. In this work, we utilize a hybrid quantum-classical workflow for investigating carbene formation in representative diazirine-diazomethane systems. Our approach leverages Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) and its extended variant, Extended Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (Ext-SQD), for ground- and excited-state analysis, combined with classical tools for geometry optimization, active-space selection, and diagnostic evaluation. Quantum computations were carried out on superconducting quantum processors, and results for both aliphatic and aryl-substituted diazirine-diazomethane pairs were benchmarked against established classical methods, including density functional theory (DFT), coupled cluster with singles and doubles (CCSD), complete active space configuration interaction (CASCI), and selected configuration interaction (SCI). SQD achieves accuracy surpassing the chemical accuracy threshold for nearly all stationary points on the potential energy surface of parent diazirine relative to the CASCI(12,10) reference, and remains close to chemical accuracy for phenyl-substituted diazirine in a (30,30) active space, with an average deviation of 1.1 kcal/mol relative to the SCI benchmark. SQD closely follows CASCI and SCI trends, showing consistent agreement. The findings demonstrate the promise of quantum computing frameworks in modeling photochemical transformations of electronically complex and pharmacologically relevant molecules.
papers.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

papers.title: Optimizing QAOA circuit transpilation with parity twine and SWAP network encodings
papers.abstract: Mapping quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) circuits with nontrivial connectivity in fixed-layout quantum platforms, such as superconducting quantum processing units (QPUs), requires a transpilation process to match the circuit to the hardware layout. This step is critical for reducing error rates on noisy QPUs. Two approaches that improve the resources required for such transpilation are the SWAP network and parity twine chains (PTC), which reduce the two-qubit gate count and circuit depth needed to represent fully connected circuits. In this work, we introduce a simulated annealing-based method that further reduces the encoding overhead of PTC and SWAP networks for QAOA circuits with nonfully connected two-qubit interactions.
